Remedi health information · Facial asymmetry

Facial asymmetry

From causes to when assessment may be needed

If differences between the two sides of your face concern you, start by understanding the changes. This guide explains possible causes, symptoms and points to discuss during an assessment.

Overview Causes Patterns & checklist Diagnosis & treatment FAQs Care at Remedi

01 · Overview

What is facial asymmetry?

Facial asymmetry is a difference in size, shape, height or position between the two sides of the face. [1]

Mild differences between the two sides are common. Having facial asymmetry does not, by itself, mean that treatment is needed. [1]

Asymmetry may be limited to one area of the face or appear in several areas at once. For example, eyebrow heights may differ while the chin remains centered. Alternatively, the chin may shift to one side while the midlines of the lips and teeth also appear different.

Areas considered when assessing facial asymmetry

1. Eye and eyebrow height
Assessment considers eyebrow height, eyelid shape and differences in soft tissue around the eyes. Eyes that appear different in size are not necessarily caused by structural differences in the eye sockets or skull.
2. Alignment of the nose and midface
Assessment considers the direction of the nose, the surrounding contours, and the prominence of the cheekbones and cheeks. Nasal asymmetry and skeletal differences in the midface should be assessed separately.
3. Position of the lips and mouth corners
The heights of the mouth corners may differ at rest and when smiling. Several factors can be involved, including movement of the muscles around the lips, the bite and jaw position.
4. Chin position and lower-jaw shape
The chin may appear shifted to one side, or one jaw angle may look more prominent. Assessment should distinguish differences in the shape of the jawbone from those related to lower-jaw position or movement.
5. Dental midlines and the bite
The midlines of the upper and lower front teeth may not align, or the lower jaw may move to one side during chewing. It is important to assess tooth alignment, the bite and jaw movement together.

Facial asymmetry often cannot be explained by a single cause. Assessment begins by distinguishing differences in appearance from actual functional difficulties. [1] [2]

Differences in appearance and functional discomfort should be considered together. This page provides general health information; an examination is needed to assess your individual causes and whether treatment is necessary.

02 · Causes

Main causes of facial asymmetry

Facial asymmetry may be associated with various factors, including skeletal development, teeth and the bite, jaw joints and chewing muscles, and soft tissue.

1. Congenital and growth-related skeletal asymmetry

Facial bones develop during growth, and the two sides may not grow to exactly the same extent.

Differences in the size or position of the upper and lower jaws, chin deviation and differences between the two jaw angles may contribute to asymmetric facial contours.

In these cases, assessment should consider the shape and position of the jawbones and how the teeth fit together, rather than the facial surface alone. If skeletal asymmetry is suspected, assessment by an orthodontist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon may be needed. [1] [2]

2. Differences in tooth alignment and the bite

The alignment of the teeth and the way the upper and lower teeth fit together may affect the position and movement of the lower jaw.

For example, if the bite differs between the two sides or the lower jaw shifts to one side when the teeth meet, facial alignment may appear different when closing the mouth or chewing.

However, a mismatch between dental midlines alone does not establish asymmetry of the jawbones themselves. Tooth alignment and the structural position of the jaw should be assessed separately. [1] [2]

3. Functional differences in the jaw joints and chewing muscles

The jaw joints allow the lower jaw to move, while the surrounding chewing muscles are involved in functions such as chewing and opening the mouth.

If there is jaw-joint pain, restricted movement, deviation when opening the mouth or differences in chewing-muscle tension, facial movement and discomfort around the jaw can be assessed together.

However, a temporomandibular disorder does not necessarily cause facial asymmetry, and jaw-joint symptoms alone cannot establish structural changes in the facial bones. [3]

4. Differences in soft tissue and muscles

Facial contours are influenced not only by bone but also by soft tissue, including skin, subcutaneous fat and muscles.

Differences in cheek volume, development of the chewing muscles, and skin or subcutaneous tissue may make the two sides of the face look different.

In these cases, it is important to distinguish skeletal differences from differences in appearance arising from soft tissue. [2]

5. Injury and acquired changes

Assessment may also include a history of injury to the face or jaw, changes following dental treatment and conditions affecting the jaw-joint area.

If previously subtle asymmetry becomes more noticeable over time, or the size or shape of one side of the face changes, the cause should be assessed rather than treating it solely as a cosmetic concern. [1] [2]

6. Posture and daily habits

Habits such as chewing on one side, clenching the teeth, sleeping position, and neck and shoulder tension can be considered when assessing strain on the jaw and surrounding muscles.

However, a particular posture or habit alone does not establish that the facial bones have become misaligned. Managing daily habits and assessing the causes of actual skeletal asymmetry should be approached separately. [1] [3]

03 · Patterns & self-check

Consider facial differences alongside any discomfort

Patterns of facial asymmetry

Facial asymmetry can be described in several ways, depending on the areas involved and whether differences are more noticeable at rest or during movement.

The categories below are explanations to aid understanding. They are not a standardized diagnostic system that assigns every patient to one specific type.

Type A. Chin deviation

The center of the lower jaw or the chin appears shifted to one side of the facial midline.

  • The chin appears shifted to the left or right
  • The left and right contours of the lower jaw appear different
  • The upper and lower dental midlines may appear misaligned
  • Differences in lower-jaw movement may be observed when chewing or opening the mouth

With this pattern, the shape and position of the lower jawbone, the bite and jaw-joint movement should be assessed separately.

Type B. Asymmetry of the mouth corners or smile

Differences may be subtle at rest, but one mouth corner rises higher or the lips move differently when smiling or speaking.

  • One corner of the mouth appears higher
  • The center of the lips shifts to one side when smiling
  • The smile appears tilted to one side in photos
  • Movement around the lips and the amount of visible teeth differ between the two sides

These differences may involve several factors, including facial-muscle movement, the teeth and bite, and jaw position. The cause cannot be determined from mouth-corner height alone.

Type C. Cheekbone and midface asymmetry

The prominence of the cheekbones, cheek volume or contours around the nose differ between the two sides.

  • One cheekbone appears more prominent
  • Cheek volume or contours appear different on the two sides
  • The left and right sides of the midface appear different in width
  • The center of the face appears shifted to one side in frontal photos

Differences in skeletal shape and soft tissue can look similar from the outside, so they need to be distinguished.

Type D. Eyebrow and eye-area asymmetry

Differences in eyebrow height, eyelid shape or soft tissue around the eyes make the eyes appear different in size or level.

A difference in apparent eye size does not necessarily mean skull asymmetry. Eyelid changes and eye-related causes should also be considered.

Type E. Combined facial asymmetry

Asymmetry is observed in several areas at once, such as chin deviation, differences in mouth-corner height and cheekbone prominence.

In these cases, the appearance of a single area cannot easily explain the causes affecting the whole face. It is important to assess the skeleton, bite, jaw movement and soft tissue separately.

    04 · Diagnosis & treatment options

    What is assessed during a facial asymmetry consultation?

    Assessment of facial asymmetry considers not only visible differences between the two sides but also when changes appeared, jaw function, the bite and accompanying symptoms.

    The following are general assessment items. For the scope of consultations at Remedi, see care information.

    1. Step 1. Review when changes began and how they developed

      Assessment includes when the differences between the two sides first concerned you and whether they have been present since childhood or appeared recently.

      A history of injuries, dental treatment and jaw-joint symptoms is also reviewed. Earlier photographs, if available, may help in understanding the pattern of changes. [1] [3]

    2. Step 2. Observe the shape of both sides of the face

      Assessment observes differences in key areas, including the eyebrows and eye area, nose, cheekbones, mouth corners, chin and jawline. [1] [2]

      Where needed, assessment may include differences during movements such as smiling or opening the mouth, as well as the face at rest.

      Photographs can be used as observation records, but apparent differences may vary with the camera angle, facial expression and lens distortion. Photos alone therefore do not establish a cause.

    3. Step 3. Assess jaw movement and chewing function

      Assessment considers opening and closing the mouth, jaw deviation, discomfort during chewing and pain around the jaw joints.

      When appropriate, chewing-muscle tension and tenderness, and neck and shoulder discomfort may also be assessed. These findings alone, however, cannot diagnose structural skeletal asymmetry. [3]

    4. Step 4. Distinguish bite-related and structural concerns

      Assessment determines whether differences in dental midlines and the bite, or the shape and position of the jawbones, require further evaluation.

      If skeletal asymmetry or problems with tooth alignment or the bite are suspected, assessment by an orthodontist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon may be needed. Imaging is determined by clinical need rather than performed routinely for every patient. [2] [3]

    5. Step 5. Establish individual care goals

      Assessment distinguishes concerns about facial appearance from functional discomfort, such as jaw movement or pain, and explains what can be evaluated in your current condition.

      Even when seeking an improvement in appearance, it is important to clarify what can be targeted, what changes may be difficult to achieve and whether further assessment is needed.

    How do approaches to facial asymmetry treatment differ?

    Treatment for facial asymmetry depends on its causes and the goals of care. Improving facial appearance and managing jaw-joint pain or function are different treatment goals.

    If differences are mild and cause no discomfort

    Specific treatment may not be necessary if there are no significant concerns about appearance or function. Decisions about treatment consider the cause and the discomfort you experience. [1]

    If there is functional discomfort in the jaw joints or chewing muscles

    If there is pain around the jaw joints, difficulty opening the mouth or chewing-muscle tension, the cause of those symptoms can be assessed and conservative care considered.

    Changes to daily habits, appropriate exercises and physical approaches to care may be considered according to the symptoms. This does not mean that such care corrects skeletal facial asymmetry. [3]

    If skeletal or bite-related differences are suspected

    Suspected differences in jawbone size or position, or problems with the way the teeth fit together, may require structural assessment by an orthodontist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon.

    Treatment options are determined by considering the cause and degree of asymmetry, stage of growth and functional problems. Not all asymmetry requires orthodontic treatment or surgery. [2]

    If soft-tissue differences and appearance are your main concerns

    If your main concern is facial volume, muscle shape or differences in soft tissue between the two sides, the characteristics and causes affecting those areas should be assessed first.

    The range of changes that can be expected varies by treatment method. Managing soft-tissue differences is not the same as treatment that changes skeletal shape. [2]

    About cranial correction and oral appliances

    Cranial orthoses and corrective appliances should be distinguished according to who they are intended for and their purpose.

    Cranial orthoses used for conditions such as positional plagiocephaly or brachycephaly in infants are intended to manage particular skull deformities. Their use cannot be generalized as a proven method for reducing adult facial or midface size, or for correcting adult facial asymmetry. [5]

    Oral appliances also have different purposes depending on their type and indications. An appropriate clinician should assess the teeth and bite, jaw-joint symptoms or oral structural problems before deciding whether an appliance is suitable. [3]

    It is therefore important to ask which structures an appliance is intended to address and for what purpose, rather than assuming it will correct all left-to-right facial differences or definitively reposition the facial bones.

    05 · Frequently asked questions

    Frequently asked questions about facial asymmetry

    What causes facial asymmetry?

    Facial asymmetry may involve various factors, including facial-bone growth and shape, tooth alignment and the bite, jaw joints and chewing muscles, and soft tissue. Appearance alone does not establish a cause, so the onset and accompanying symptoms should also be considered. [1] [2]

    How can I check facial asymmetry myself?

    You can observe eyebrow and eye height, the direction of the nose, cheekbone and jawline shape, mouth-corner height and jaw movement. However, differences seen in a mirror or photographs may vary with viewing or photographic conditions, and a self-check alone cannot establish the cause or need for treatment. [1]

    Related reading · Facial asymmetry in photos: why it looks different from the mirror

    Are temporomandibular disorders and facial asymmetry the same?

    They are different concepts. Facial asymmetry refers to differences in the shape or position of the two sides of the face. Temporomandibular disorders encompass conditions involving pain or dysfunction in the jaw joints and chewing muscles. The two may occur together, but do not necessarily accompany each other. [2] [3]

    Does chewing on one side cause facial asymmetry?

    Chewing on one side is one factor to consider when assessing strain on the jaw and chewing muscles. However, this habit alone does not establish that the facial bones have developed asymmetrically. Other possible factors, including existing bite differences, pain and dental problems, should also be assessed.

    Changing habits alone also cannot be assumed to correct skeletal asymmetry. Managing habits that put strain on the jaw and assessing structural causes should be considered separately. [1] [3]

    Can headaches or shoulder pain also be caused by facial asymmetry?

    Headaches and neck or shoulder pain can have many causes, including musculoskeletal and neurological problems. Related symptoms may be assessed when jaw-joint or chewing-muscle discomfort is also present. However, headaches or shoulder pain alone do not establish facial asymmetry as the cause. [3] [6]

    Does facial asymmetry always need treatment?

    Mild asymmetry is common. Treatment may not be needed if there are no significant concerns about appearance or function. If changes concern you or you have functional discomfort, discuss the possible causes with a clinician. [1]

    Do jaw sounds mean I need treatment for asymmetry?

    Jaw-joint sounds without pain are common and do not, by themselves, require treatment. It is helpful to check whether pain, restricted movement or locking also occurs. [3]

    Can facial asymmetry be made completely symmetrical?

    Treatment outcomes depend on the cause and degree of asymmetry and the method used. Some differences may remain after treatment, and managing functional discomfort is a different goal from changing skeletal shape. It is important to discuss expected changes and limitations before treatment. [1]

    What should I do if one side of my face suddenly droops?

    Sudden drooping on one side of the face, difficulty smiling, slurred speech, or weakness in an arm or leg on one side may indicate an emergency such as stroke. Call 119 immediately for emergency assessment, even if the symptoms go away shortly afterward. [4]

    06 · Care at Remedi

    Facial asymmetry consultations at Kyung Hee Remedi Korean Medicine Clinic in Mapo

    When differences between the two sides of your face concern you, simply identifying which side is larger or higher may not be enough.

    In facial asymmetry consultations, Kyung Hee Remedi Korean Medicine Clinic first asks about the areas and discomfort that concern you most, then considers the shape of both sides of the face, jaw movement, chewing-muscle tension, neck and shoulder discomfort, and daily habits together.

    However, not all visible differences arise from muscles or posture. If skeletal or bite-related problems, a jaw-joint condition or another medical cause is suspected, assessment in the relevant field may be needed.

    What to prepare before your consultation

    • When you first noticed differences between the two sides of your face
    • Areas of particular concern: eyes, cheekbones, mouth corners, chin, jawline and others
    • Discomfort when opening your mouth or chewing
    • Jaw-joint pain or sounds, and any limited mouth opening
    • A history of facial or jaw injuries and dental treatment
    • Existing scan images or related medical records

    Questions to discuss during your consultation

    • Assessment of your current condition and possible approaches to care
    • The purpose of treatment, possible changes and limitations
    • Whether additional tests or assessment by another specialty are needed

    During your consultation, it is helpful to discuss the assessment of your current condition, possible approaches to care, the purpose and limitations of treatment, and whether additional tests are needed.

    Kyung Hee Remedi Korean Medicine Clinic explains the assessment and care options needed based on each patient's concerns and condition.

    Skeletal or bite-related problems and sudden neurological symptoms may require assessment in the relevant field. Specific treatment methods, duration and costs should be discussed after an examination.
